title: Blessing the house
hookLine: many churches bless homes at Epiphany or when people move in

lines: A PASTOR IN AN EMPTY ROOM.
cards: Above a door, in white chalk, a short line of numbers and letters with little crosses between them. It went up one winter afternoon, while someone stood on a kitchen chair.
A few streets away, a couple has just carried the last box into a new apartment, and their pastor stands in the empty living room, reading a short passage aloud.
Across town, an Orthodox priest moves from room to room with a sprig of green dipped in water, sprinkling the walls, the beds, the stove. Three homes. One old habit.

teach.h: FIRST SAY, PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.
teach.b: When Jesus sends his followers out to the towns in Luke, he tells them what to do at the door: "And into whatsoever house ye enter, first say, Peace be to this house." First, before teaching or supper.
If a person of peace lives there, the peace will rest on them; if not, it comes back to you. Nothing is wasted. Next, the chalk.
Around Epiphany, the feast of the wise men, some Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran households mark the door with the year and three letters.
Tradition says they stand for the names later given to the wise men, Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar, and also for Latin words asking Christ to bless the house.

teach.h: CHALK FOR THE WISE MEN'S HOUSE.
teach.b: Matthew says the wise men came to a house: "when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother." The chalk remembers a house where Christ was found. Then, the water.
Orthodox churches bless water at Theophany, the feast of Christ's baptism, and afterward priests visit homes to sprinkle it through each room, with prayers for the people who live there.

Other churches bless a home when a family moves in, room by room. Last, a house that changed. Zacchaeus, a tax collector the crowd grumbles about, climbs a tree to see Jesus, and Jesus invites himself over.
By the end, Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house." Not to the bricks: to the man, and the household. Walls don't need peace.
The people who argue in that kitchen and make up in it do. A blessing asks that this ordinary place be one where God is welcome.

how: Some Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran households chalk their doors at Epiphany; Orthodox priests visit homes with water blessed at Theophany; and other churches offer a house blessing when a family moves in.

o: asking God's peace on a home and the people in it
a priest's yearly check that a home is kept holy
cleaning a new house before the family moves in

games.q: blessing the house — tap the pairs.
p: what to say first at the door

s: Jesus told his followers to teach first, then offer peace
"first say, Peace be to this house." peace came before anything else.
in Matthew, the wise men came into a house
"when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother."
Jesus waited for Zacchaeus to invite him
Jesus invited himself: "to day I must abide at thy house."

games.q: you're Jesus, passing through Jericho. a tax collector the crowd grumbles about has climbed a tree to see you. everyone is watching. what do you do?
o: call him down and invite yourself to his house.
tell him to come back when he's changed.
games.why: "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." by the end, salvation has come to that house.

practice: Walk slowly through your home, or walk it in your mind, pausing at the front door and then in each room, thinking of what happens there, and who.
If you pray, you can say at each doorway, peace be to this house; if you don't, let each pause be a wish of peace for whoever lives there. End where you started, at the door.

wordCard.voice: Blessing the house. Asking God's peace on a home and the people in it, with words, chalk or water.

orig.note: Greek: peace, the word Jesus tells his followers to say first at the door in Luke 10:5.

carryVoice: Your line: peace to this house. Peace for the people inside. Until tomorrow.
